units: a teacher points out to her student that the tool warps whenever the applied force changes
she asks him to run the movement again in slow motion
the student says he followed the written instructions
the student admits he did not understand the wording of the last point
the teacher explains that heat expands the metal and throws off the measurement
she states that the origin of a fault is rarely found where it shows
the student notices that the cutting waste curls badly
the student concludes on his own that the angle of the tool must change
the teacher considers this reasoning transferable to other machines
she holds that a trade is handed on through an understanding of cause and effect
text: The instructor tells her apprentice that the blade warps the moment his wrist presses harder. She has him set the tool down and repeat the entire movement at half speed. He protests that he followed the written sheet exactly, though the final instruction never quite made sense to him. She unpacks it: the hand leans in early, the workpiece overheats, the metal expands, and the measurement comes out false. A fault, she adds, seldom begins where it eventually becomes visible. The apprentice studies the shaving emerging from the groove and remarks that it curls badly. Then he reaches the conclusion himself, that the cutting angle must change. She approves, and promises that once such reasoning becomes habit, it transfers to every machine in the workshop. A trade, she concludes, passes from one person to another through cause and effect, never through imitated gestures.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: knowledge once rested on human memory alone
the death of a teacher meant that part of his doctrine disappeared
learned communities looked for a lasting safeguard
reciting as a group spread the effort of memory across several people
an error by one reciter was caught by another
writing under dictation then secured what speech preserved badly
the method called for trained copyists and a term by term check of the text
copying mistakes became the new danger
checking by two readers comparing aloud corrected that flaw
piling up these precautions made the doctrine transmissible over long stretches of time
text: Before writing, learning survived in human memory alone, and that left it badly exposed. When a teacher died, part of what he taught went into the ground with him. Communities of scholars looked for a safeguard that would outlast any single life. They settled first on reciting in chorus, which spread the burden of holding things across many mouths instead of one. Where a voice faltered, another voice held the line, and the whole came through. Dictation followed, fixing on a surface what speech kept so poorly. The method called for trained copyists and for a check made term by term against the text. Mistakes of the hand now replaced mistakes of the tongue as the chief danger. Against that, two readers would take the copies and compare them aloud. Precaution laid on precaution is why a body of teaching could cross many lifetimes without warping.

units: two ways of teaching hand skills exist side by side
the first has the trainer perform before the learner who then copies
this route suits continuous movements that words convey badly
it leaves the learner helpless once conditions change
the second names and justifies every step
it demands more effort at the outset
it supplies a rule that can be reused in other settings
seasoned trainers blend the two approaches
they ask the learner to describe for himself the movement he has just seen
alternating between watching and speaking anchors the learning more firmly
text: Two ways of teaching hand skills sit side by side, and neither one wins everywhere. The first is showing. The trainer does the work, the learner watches, then tries it. This carries smooth flowing movement quickly, the kind that words handle badly. Its weakness shows up as soon as the setting shifts, since the learner is left with nothing to steer by. The second is telling. Every step gets a name, a place in the order, and a reason. It costs more at the start, but it hands the learner a rule that travels to other jobs. Trainers with years behind them use both. They run through the movement, then make the learner tell it back in his own words. Swinging between the eye and the mouth holds the learning down far better than either route on its own. So the comparison names no winner. It names a mixture.

units: a neighbor recounts his early days in the workshop of a relative
he arranges his account around three memories
he had been given the most unsteady workbench
he understood that the faulty furniture was part of the trial imposed on him
he reversed a pattern he was meant to copy and ruined a stack of boards
the blunder still amuses the crew
no colleague gave him any explanation unprompted
everything came unstuck once he started questioning the old hands
the old hands would answer provided they were asked
he now passes this lesson on to the beginners he supervises
text: The fellow down the hall described his first week in his uncle's workshop, and it reduces to three memories. The bench, first. They handed him the wobbliest one available, the one that rocked whenever he leaned on it, and he understood soon enough that the bench belonged to the trial. The stencil, second. Sent to mark a stack of boards, he laid the pattern down backwards and ruined the entire pile, which the crew still recalls with amusement. The silence, third. Nobody explained anything. They put a tool in his hand and waited. Eventually he began asking questions, and everything opened at once. The old hands answered willingly, they simply wanted the question first. He passes that lesson to the beginners under his supervision, that whoever stays silent learns twice as slowly.

units: the session opens with the handing out of materials to the participants
each one receives an untreated piece of wood and a stiff card template
the participants check that the corner is true with a measuring instrument
warped pieces are pulled out at this stage
the outline of the template is traced in one unbroken line
the teacher makes uneven tracings start over
after a break the measurements are carried over to the other face
this transfer brings any drift into the open at once
the session ends with a shared showing of the corrected mistakes
the cutting is put off until the next meeting
text: It opens with the handout, in the training rooms where marking out is taught. Each person gets a rough board and a template cut from stiff card. Next comes the square. The participants set it against the edge and make sure the corner is true, and any board that has twisted is pulled out right there. Then the line. The template is traced with a fine point, and the hand never lifts partway through. The trainer walks the aisles and sends anyone whose line wanders back to the start of it. A break follows. Afterwards each person carries the measurements over to the far face, which brings any drift into the open at once. The session closes with everyone gathered round, each participant holding up a board and naming the mistake he put right. Nothing gets cut until the group meets again.

units: adults take up writing again in the basement of a former storage building
they had given up writing a very long time ago
an association of neighbors lends the premises for nothing
the absence of official oversight spares newcomers the feeling of going back to school
the woman in charge holds that embarrassment discourages more than the difficulty of the subject
the layout of the room makes voices carry
the participants therefore hear one another read
this mutual listening breeds a rivalry among them
a former factory worker moved from copying to writing on her own
every stage of her progress rests on the one before it
text: In the low room beneath an old storehouse, a handful of adults are writing again after letting decades pass without it. A neighborhood association lends the space and asks nothing in return, and that plain generosity accomplishes what no budget could. Because the room answers to no authority, nobody entering feels she is returning to school. The woman running the evening states it plainly, that embarrassment drives more people away than difficulty ever does. The tables are broad, the ceiling high, so voices travel, and because voices travel, everyone hears the others reading aloud. Out of that listening a quiet rivalry emerges. A former factory worker copied first, then dictated to the woman beside her, then wrote unaided. The chain advances slowly, yet each link holds because the previous one held.

units: this training workbench has an adjustable height
its top is drilled with holes at even spacing
beginners hold their piece badly and it drifts under the tool
pegs dropped into the holes lock the piece with no hand clamping
the top is made of a hard wood that is not abrasive to blades
a side rail stores the measuring instruments
this storage frees up the working surface
a container set underneath catches the cutting waste
this collection limits the risk of falls
a slot at the front takes the learner's instruction cards
text: The first thing you notice about a training bench is that it rises and drops to fit the worker, and that its top is drilled with holes at even spacing. Those holes answer an old trouble. A beginner grips the work poorly, it wanders under the tool, and the cut runs off the line. Drop pegs into the holes and the piece sits still, with no vice and no straining fingers. The top is solid beech, dense enough to take a knock, soft enough to leave a cutting edge alone. A rail along one side holds the square and the rule, so they stay within reach instead of littering the surface. Underneath, a tray catches the shavings and offcuts, which keeps the floor from turning slippery. A groove across the front takes the learner's instruction cards. Every part of it answers something a beginner was seen struggling with.

units: learning by heart and learning by inquiry are often presented as incompatible
the author judges this rivalry to be groundless
with nothing held in mind the learner only tries at random
the learner who stops at memory recites a table of contents without knowing what it holds
these two figures fail because they pull apart operations that belong together
memorizing demands an effort at the start and then frees one
it makes attention available for more demanding operations
inquiry stays costly at every stage
it teaches one to state a claim, to test it and to give it up
the author recommends combining the two rather than choosing
text: Learning by heart and learning by inquiry are set against each other far too readily, as though one had to drive the other out. The quarrel strikes me as badly framed. A learner holding nothing in mind does not inquire at all. He gropes, having no material to put together. A learner who has only committed things to memory recites a table of contents for a book he never opened. Both fail, and for one reason, that they pull apart operations the mind keeps joined. Weigh what each of them demands. Memorizing takes its toll early and repays later, since it frees attention for work of a higher order. Inquiry charges at every stage, yet it trains a person to state a claim, put it to the test, and give it up. One yields speed, the other caution. A serious training measures out both and declines to choose.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: none of her relatives had practiced a craft trade before her
her path breaks down into three parts
she began her apprenticeship while her friends were still studying
she learned above all by watching an older practitioner who said little
she repairs damaged books and remakes the worn parts
she turns down orders that call for too short a deadline
she first builds a model in ordinary paper to test her decisions
she deliberately limits her teaching to two students a season
this limit lets her correct movements on the spot
she refuses to write a book, holding that the craft passes from hand to hand
text: No one in her family had worked with their hands before her. The life of this bookbinder falls into three parts. Training came first. She signed on as an apprentice at an age when her friends were still sitting in classrooms, and she learned by watching the hands of an older woman who said very little. Then the work itself. She brings damaged volumes back, resews the gatherings, rebuilds the worn headbands, and turns away any order that comes with a rushed deadline. Before a delicate repair she builds the whole volume again in ordinary paper, so she can test a choice without risking the original. Teaching came last. Two students a season enter her workshop, never more, because she means to catch every movement as it happens. She will not write a manual. One hand, she says, teaches another hand.

units: the author comes out of this woodcraft course with a divided judgment
the opening sessions won him over
a booklet handed out at the start announced a route one could follow
the instructor moved at a pace the novices could bear
the number of participants grew because sign-ups were accepted too late
the trainees had to wait for want of enough tools
a good share of the sessions went by watching the others
the person in charge split the group to put things right
the author holds that this decision came too late
he recommends the course only if numbers are capped in advance
text: Honestly, I came out of that woodworking course in two minds about it, so let me take it in order. The early sessions won me over. We were handed a booklet whose contents page laid out a route you could follow, and the woman teaching kept things moving without leaving the raw beginners behind. Then the group swelled, because sign-ups were still being taken far too late. From that point on you queued for the one saw in the room, and half the session went by watching other people work. The organizer did react and split us in two, which I was glad of, but it came late. The last few sessions clawed back a little of what had been lost. I would send someone there on one condition, that the numbers be capped when the sign-up opens. The material is sound. The running of it is not.
